summary:
Earth Trend Detective is a free web app that answers one question for any place on Earth: is it really changing here, or is it just noise? Click a spot on the globe, pick one of nearly 30 variables (air temperature, rain, soil water, sea ice, ocean chlorophyll, vegetation greenness and more) and get a verdict built on NASA data and real statistics: a regression with a 95% confidence range plus a Mann-Kendall test corrected for year-to-year memory. The app warns when a record is too short, flips direction or hides opposite trends inside one area, and the nearest NOAA weather station acts as a second witness.

Every result is explained in plain English or Bangla, including why the change matters for people and nature. A Time Machine plays NASA satellite imagery year by year next to the chart and marks real fires, storms and floods from NASA EONET.

Trend claims spread faster than the evidence behind them. Our tool lets students, journalists and local planners test a claim for their own place in a minute, and see both what the data shows and what it cannot prove.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Earth Trend Detective turns NASA Earth data into an honest, plain-language answer to "is this really changing here?"

- Investigate: click anywhere on the globe (or open a whole-planet record such as sea level or Arctic sea ice), choose a variable, a year range, and one month or the yearly average. The app fetches the data, runs the trend tests and gives a verdict ("Clear trend", "Maybe a trend" or "No clear trend") with the total change, the change per decade and the place named, for example "near Dhaka, Bangladesh".

- Time Machine: NASA GIBS satellite imagery of the same variable plays year by year on the globe while a cursor moves along the chart. Record years light up, and real natural events from NASA EONET appear as dots in the year they happened.

- Why it matters: for each variable, a short note on what the change tends to do to people and nature, with everyday comparisons calculated from the data. Example: the Arctic's September sea ice fell 46% from 1979 to 2026; the ice lost covers an area about 3.5 times the size of Egypt. Greenland lost about 6,100 gigatonnes of ice from 2002 to 2026, which alone raised global sea level by about 17 mm.

- Deeper checks: a second witness (the nearest long-running NOAA weather station, tested the same way), a map of opposite trends inside the area (each grid cell tested on its own), a split of the record into thirds (speeding up, slowing down or reversing), a one-click check-up of 8 variables at one place, a compare mode, 12 ready-made case files and CSV export of every number.

- Optional AI coach: explains a result in simple English or Bangla, using only numbers the server calculated.

HOW IT WORKS

- A Python (FastAPI) server fetches the data from NASA services and caches every response, so the demo keeps working on bad Wi-Fi once a place has been opened.

- Statistics: yearly means; a straight-line fit with a 95% confidence band; the Mann-Kendall test with the Hamed-Rao correction, which drives the verdict so that neighbouring years that resemble each other cannot fake a trend; Sen's slope; and Weatherhead's estimate of how many years of data a trend of that size needs. The verdict sentences come from fixed rules applied to these numbers, never from AI.

- Plain-language warnings appear when the record is short, the direction changed halfway, years are missing, or the simple and corrected tests disagree.

- The globe is CesiumJS showing time-stepped NASA GIBS layers, with Natural Earth borders and city names. Charts are Plotly.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- Anyone can check a climate claim for their own place in about a minute, without downloading data or writing code.

- It teaches the difference between a real trend and natural ups and downs, which is where most public confusion about climate data starts.

- Bangla support and Bangladesh case files serve one of the world's most climate-exposed countries, where most people do not read science in English.

- Students, journalists and local planners get evidence they can cite: every result names its dataset and links to the source.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES AND SOFTWARE

Python 3.14 (FastAPI, uvicorn, NumPy, SciPy, pymannkendall, requests, h5py); JavaScript, HTML and CSS with CesiumJS and Plotly.js, with no build step; Playwright for end-to-end tests. Claude Code was used as a coding assistant and the Claude API powers the optional coach. No hardware.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

- It treats a trend like a detective case: a verdict, a second witness, warnings when the evidence is weak, and the events that happened at the scene.

- The Time Machine links three things that usually live apart: satellite imagery, the statistical trend and the real events of each year.

- It shows what the data cannot say as clearly as what it can: opposite trends hidden inside one average, changes that are big but uncertain, and a note on every event list that events are records, not proof of cause.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

- Validity: every number comes from real NASA or NOAA data; nothing is simulated. The verdict uses a test that allows for year-to-year memory. When the map layer is a different quantity from the numbers, the app says so.

- Honesty about causes: explanations say what a change "tends to" do, and the event list notes that NASA's event tracking has grown since about 2015, so recent years look busier partly because of better records.

- Data quirks we found and fixed: daily satellite swaths with gaps replaced by gap-free monthly layers; flood outlines with latitude and longitude swapped put back in the right place; planned (prescribed) burns removed from wildfire records.

- Accessibility: plain language, two languages, keyboard controls (Space plays, arrow keys step through years), readable text sizes and a layout that fits phones.

- Security: API keys stay on the server and are never sent to the browser.

MERRA-2 reanalysis (NASA GMAO), via POWER and GIBS
CERES radiation and UV index (NASA LaRC), via POWER and GIBS
GISTEMP v4 global surface temperature (NASA GISS)
NASA-SSH Global Mean Sea Level indicator (PO.DAAC)
GRACE/GRACE-FO Greenland ice mass time series (JPL mascons, PO.DAAC)
GRACE/GRACE-FO Antarctica ice mass time series (JPL mascons, PO.DAAC)
MODIS Terra vegetation index MOD13Q1 v6.1
MODIS Terra land surface temperature MOD11A2 v6.1
ORNL DAAC MODIS subset web service
NASA EONET (Earth Observatory Natural Event Tracker)
AIRS relative humidity imagery (NASA JPL), via GIBS
GHRSST MUR sea ice concentration (JPL, PO.DAAC), via GIBS
projectRefs: NSIDC Sea Ice Index v4 (G02135, NOAA@NSIDC)
NOAA NCEI Global Summary of the Month (weather stations)
GDACS disaster reports (linked from NASA EONET events)
Natural Earth (borders and place names, public domain)
Weatherhead et al. (1998), years needed to detect a trend
IPCC AR6 WG1 Summary for Policymakers (background for "why it matters")
